readings.title: The Cow
readings.challenge: Hear a child thank a cow and then give her advice.
readings.focus: The child thanks the cow for her milk and tells her where to eat, so the milk will stay sweet.
readings.context: Ann and Jane Taylor wrote these rhymes for young children about two hundred years ago. Hemlock is a poisonous weed; rank means growing thick and coarse. Cowslips are yellow wildflowers; to dine is to eat dinner.

excerpt.locator: “The Cow,” the complete poem; opens “Thank you, pretty cow, that made Pleasant milk to soak my bread, Ev’ry day, and ev’ry…”; closes “…bubbling water flows, Where the grass is fresh and fine, Pretty cow, go there and dine.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the child thank the cow?
facilitatorNotes: For the milk that soaks the child’s bread, every day and every night.
evidence: Thank you, pretty cow, that made
Pleasant milk to soak my bread,

questions.prompt: What should the cow not eat, and what should she eat instead?
facilitatorNotes: Not the hemlock on the weedy bank, but the yellow cowslips, which will make her milk sweet.
evidence: Do not chew the hemlock rank,

questions.prompt: Describe the place where the child tells the cow to go and dine. Why might a good meadow make good milk?
facilitatorNotes: Where violets grow, water bubbles and the grass is fresh and fine. A child who connects good food with good milk is following the poem’s idea.
evidence: Pretty cow, go there and dine.

readings.title: The Sparrows
readings.challenge: Hear a child try to make friends with shy birds.
readings.focus: A child promises the nest-building sparrows that she only wants to watch them, never to cage them.
readings.context: Sparrows are small brown birds that build untidy nests. A jenneting tree is an early apple tree. “Dick” was a pet name for a bird. Read gently, as if not to frighten the birds away.

excerpt.locator: “The Sparrows,” the complete poem; opens “Hop about, pretty sparrows, and pick up the hay, And the twigs, and the wool, and the…”; closes “…be! Then come, pretty bird, while I quietly stand At the foot of the jenneting tree.”.

questions.prompt: What are the sparrows picking up, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Hay, twigs, wool and moss to build their nest, their “house.”
evidence: Hop about, pretty sparrows, and pick up the hay,
How you gather the twigs for your house;

questions.prompt: What does the child promise not to do?
facilitatorNotes: Not to catch them and fasten them in a cage, where they would hop all day on a stick or flutter in a rage.
evidence: I don’t mean to catch you, you dear little Dick,
And fasten you up in a cage;

questions.prompt: What would make the child happiest? Do you think the sparrows will come?
facilitatorNotes: If a sparrow would eat a crumb from her hand. The poem does not say whether one comes; children can guess, perhaps saying she must stand very still.
evidence: Oh dear, if you’d eat a crumb out of my hand,
Then come, pretty bird, while I quietly stand

readings.title: A Wasp and a Bee
readings.challenge: Follow a conversation and the lesson drawn from it at the end.
readings.focus: A handsome wasp asks why people prefer the plain bee, and the bee says the trouble is the wasp’s sting.
readings.context: Wasps and bees are both striped insects that can sting, and bees make honey. Elegant means graceful; homely means plain; ill-natured means unkind; fair means good-looking. The last verse speaks to people, not to insects.

excerpt.locator: “A Wasp and a Bee,” the complete poem (the initials printed after it omitted); opens “A wasp met a bee that was just buzzing by, And he said, little cousin, can you tell me…”; closes “…the wasp, if ill-natured they are, They will never be loved, if they’re ever so fair.”.

questions.prompt: What is the wasp proud of?
facilitatorNotes: Its shining gold-yellow back and its elegant shape.
evidence: My back shines as bright and as yellow as gold,

questions.prompt: Why does the bee say people do not love the wasp?
facilitatorNotes: Because of its sting and the mischief it does, not because of its looks.
evidence: They cannot put up with, and that is your sting.

questions.prompt: The last verse turns the story into a lesson for people. What is the lesson?
facilitatorNotes: Unkind people will not be loved however good-looking they are: kindness matters more than looks. Some children will point out that bees can sting too, a fair point the poem does not answer.
evidence: Because, like the wasp, if ill-natured they are,
They will never be loved, if they’re ever so fair.
